APPENDIX 1, EXPLANATION OF TERMS, DEFINITIONS AND ADDITIONAL BACK-GROUND
Measurement and Noise Assessment Procedures. Technical definitions of acoustical terminology shall be those contained in the related current documents of the American National Standards Institute (ANSI) and the American Society for Testing and Materials (ASTM). There has been a proliferation of concepts and mathematical techniques relating to sound and human response to sound. Fundamental to most all noise assessment procedures are the physical measurement of sound pressure and the concept of a level expressed in decibels. (See Appendix 2.) 
a. Sound Pressure Level Expressed in Decibels. Noise ("unwanted sound") affects the human ear through physical changes in sound pressure superimposed on the static atmospheric pressure in the presence of sound. Sound pressure has units of force per unit area.
When a sound level meter is used, <u>Sound Pressure Level</u> can be determined and expressed in decibels, dB. In this case, the <u>decibel</u> is a logarithmic value which is referenced to the <u>faintest</u> sound pressure detectable by the human ear. Those requiring a more precise definition or understanding of these terms are referred to the forthcoming HUD noise assessment manuals for further discussion.
In this circular, the decibel values, dB(A), are for those sound levels measured using the A-weighting network of a standardized sound level meter. The A-weighting network most closely approximates the response of the human ear to noise.
Relatively inexpensive and portable metering equipment is available for purchase or, in some cases, rental. Some of the portable metering equipment also permits the accumulation of time for which the noise level at the site exceeds a given decibel setting. Sound level meters shall conform to the specifications set forth in the appropriate documents of the American National Standards Institute.
The sound level meter is useful for measuring steady state or persistent noise and for identifying maximum sounds of intermittent noise. The A-weighted sound level, dB(A), has also been used as a first approximation in characterizing transportion noise. More sophisiticated evaluations of aircraft noise include some modifications which consider additional factor and are expressed as perceived noise in decibels such as PNdB or EPNdB. These refinements are discussed at greater length in the HUD noise assessment manuals.
